summary:
Our solution is an interactive platform for planning and comparing landing sites at the Moon’s south pole, making a decision-making process based on physical models and NASA data accessible to the general public.

The system integrates topography and the positions of the Sun and Earth over time. It calculates the energy available to a lunar lander from direct solar radiation and sunlight reflected from the lunar surface up to second order, while also accounting for the effects of surface temperature and thermal radiation.

At the same time, the system evaluates the availability and quality of communication with Earth, considering terrain obstructions and signal losses.

To improve simulation efficiency, we use adaptive spatial subdivision, focusing computational resources on the most significant regions.

Users can define their mission requirements and priorities through a chatbot. A cost function combines energy, communication, and terrain metrics, evaluates constraints, and ranks landing sites according to the specific needs of the mission.

In this way, SuloBeam transforms complex scientific data into an accessible tool for selecting the optimal landing location and time.
details:
What it does

Lunar Horizon is a desktop app that helps mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates near the lunar south pole. At the south pole the Sun and the Earth stay very low on the horizon, so a nearby ridge or crater rim can decide whether a lander has power and whether it can talk to Earth. Lunar Horizon takes the real terrain into account and answers two questions for any site and date: when the Sun is visible (power), and when the Earth is visible (direct-to-Earth communication).

How it works

  • Real terrain. The app reads NASA LRO LOLA elevation models directly: the polar grid at 40 m per pixel for 80°S to the pole, and the global grid for terrain beyond it. A fast function turns any latitude and longitude into the local lunar radius. It also checks slope and relief over the lander’s footprint.
  • Real positions of the Sun and Earth. The app uses JPL Horizons vector tables and NAIF SPICE kernels for the Moon’s orientation.
  • Horizon ray casting. From each site, the engine traces the terrain along great circles toward the Sun and the Earth. It computes how much of the solar disk and of the Earth disk is visible over time, including eclipses of the Sun by the Earth.
  • Power and communication. It computes the solar irradiance on the panel and a full radio link budget for the direct-to-Earth link.
  • Mission scoring. A cost function combines Earth contact time, energy and slope. The energy part uses a battery simulation plus the fraction of time in sunlight. The total score is a weighted geometric mean, so a site that completely fails one need, such as having no Earth contact, cannot score well. Every site gets a clear verdict, Good candidate, Not suitable or Incomplete data, with the reasons in plain language.

Radio quality: SINR (Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio)

Seeing the Earth is not enough. The radio signal must also be strong enough compared to the noise and interference at the receiver. For every moment in time, Lunar Horizon computes:

  • The link budget: transmit power, antenna gain, free-space path loss over the Earth-Moon distance, and receiver sensitivity (G/T).
  • The SNR, and then the SINR = signal / (noise + interference), with a user-defined level of external interference.
  • The ground-reflection effect (two-ray model): the radio wave reflected from the lunar surface interferes with the direct wave. It can strengthen or weaken the signal, especially when the Earth is low on the horizon.
  • The required SINR to reach the needed Eb/N0 at the chosen data rate. The chart shows exactly when the link closes, when it is close to failing, and when the Earth is blocked and there is no signal at all.

The interference level also feeds into the mission score and the hours-per-day table, so all parts of the app agree.

Solar radiation

For every moment in time, the app computes how much solar radiation actually reaches the lander, after terrain shadows and eclipses by the Earth:

  • On the solar panel and on a surface facing the Sun, in W/m².
  • Totals over the mission: energy in kWh/m², peak and average values, and the electricity the panel produces given its area and efficiency.
  • A choice between a fixed panel and a vertical panel that tracks the Sun. Near the pole the Sun circles just above the horizon, so a flat panel receives very little light.

Main features

  • An interactive Moon globe and a polar map with known sites: IM-1, IM-2, Artemis III candidate regions, Shackleton, Faustini and de Gerlache. The south pole is the study area.
  • An animated timeline showing the paths of the Sun and the Earth across the local sky, above the terrain silhouette. It also shows the Moon’s orbit and phase.
  • Time left until sunset and Earthset, the longest dark period, and hours per day of sunlight, Earth visibility and working radio link.
  • Charts of SINR and solar radiation over time, linked to the timeline.
  • “Land at sunrise”: the app moves the landing to the local sunrise at the chosen site, as real CLPS missions are planned.
  • Comparing and ranking sites and dates, with a rule-based mission assistant that explains the results.
  • Export to CSV and JSON, including SNR, SINR and radiation, and settings for the lander (panels, battery, radio, interference, limits).

Validation against official sources

  • IM-1 Odysseus: the app gives an elevation of 2,594 m and a slope of 12.2°. NASA reports 2,579 m and a slope of about 12° at the site where the lander tipped over.
  • IM-2 Athena: the app gives 5,322 m. LROC Quickmap gives 5,321.8 m at the same point.
  • Moon phase: the app correctly showed a 100% lit full Moon on November 24, 2026.

Impact

CLPS missions have very short lives, usually one lunar day, and depend on sunlight and a line of sight to Earth. Lunar Horizon makes these limits visible and explains them simply. It helps planners see why a site or date works or fails, and lets teachers and students explore real lunar data in an intuitive way. It is not only a tool for experts.

Tools and technologies

  • Python, PyQt6 with Qt WebEngine, NumPy, SpiceyPy, and Leaflet in JavaScript for the maps.
  • Data: NASA LRO LOLA, JPL Horizons, NAIF SPICE kernels, and LROC Quickmap for checking our results.
  • Our team’s own engine: SuloBeam, for energy and communication, including the radio link budget, the SINR and two-ray models, and solar irradiance.
  • No special hardware.

What makes it creative

  • It combines terrain, the motion of the Sun and the Earth, power, radio quality (SINR) and mission rules in one tool, instead of separate maps.
  • Every verdict comes with a human explanation, not just a number.
  • The time animation shows why light and communication come and go, not only when.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy against official data.
  • Being honest about uncertainty: the app marks data as unknown instead of guessing.
  • Realistic mission assumptions, such as landing at sunrise, vertical solar panels near the pole, and radio interference.
  • Speed on an ordinary computer.
  • Accessibility for non-experts.
